name: Bing
summary: Web search engine operated by Microsoft, presented as an AI-powered search and answer engine, with a crawler and central index, a publicly listed but unweighted set of ranking parameters, vertical experiences and AI answers, funded by labelled advertising.
license: Proprietary service (no source licence published); IndexNow protocol offered under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence

content.introduction: Bing, presented by its operator as Microsoft Bing, is the web search engine operated by Microsoft. It is a service reached through a web page, through a Bing application on mobile, or as the default engine of another browser or of Windows, and Microsoft describes it on its product page as an "AI-powered search and answer engine". Three boundaries matter for this entry. Bing is one product inside a much larger Microsoft portfolio: Copilot, Microsoft Advertising, Microsoft Edge, Bing Maps and the Bing Image Creator are related, and their properties are not automatically properties of the engine. The engine is proprietary; what Microsoft publishes in detail is guidance for site owners and a statement of ranking principles, not the ranking code. And Microsoft's own documentation is explicit that the published parameters are listed "in general order of importance" and that their relative weight varies from query to query, which is the correct level of precision available to an outside reader.
content.origin_and_history: The pages consulted for this entry describe current operation and publishing rules; none of them dates the launch of the engine, its rebranding or its corporate ownership history, and this entry therefore asserts no founding date. What the documentation does provide is dated statements of position. Microsoft's explanation of how Bing delivers search results carries a "last updated" date of 2025-03. The Microsoft Privacy Statement carries a "last updated" date of 2026-09. The Bing Webmaster Guidelines are undated but describe a current scope that includes Copilot and grounding API results alongside classic search, which shows how the documentation has been extended rather than replaced. One dated retirement is documented on Microsoft Learn: the public Bing Search and Bing Custom Search APIs were retired on 2025-08-11, so the programmatic surface that existed earlier is no longer available. Earlier history would require sources outside this set and is not attempted here.
content.rendering_engine_and_technical_architect: As a remote service, Bing has no browser engine of its own; the results page is delivered to whatever browser the user runs, and the Bing application is a separate client. The architecture that Microsoft documents is the retrieval pipeline. Bingbot crawls the web, using an algorithm to decide what to crawl and how often while trying to limit its impact on sites, and prioritising known pages that are not yet indexed or that appear to have changed. The pages it fetches are analysed and added to the Bing index, where algorithms determine which sites, articles, images and videos become eligible for given queries. Ranking then matches a query against indexed pages. Microsoft describes the ranking approach as heavily machine-learned: a model is trained on examples of ideal results to learn which features predict usefulness, using automated signals such as user interactions and training data labelled by human judges or by AI systems with human oversight. Microsoft also states that judges are guided to align with its ranking goals and that ranking systems are monitored and adjusted over time. Separately, the IndexNow protocol lets a site signal changed URLs directly rather than waiting for a crawl.
content.interface_and_documented_features: The documented interface is a results page with verticals and enhanced answer elements. Microsoft describes narrowing by category - images, videos, news and shopping - and an "Answers" layer that returns richer content above or beside the results, sometimes with a direct answer and a sidebar of related facts, and sometimes generated by AI with links to key sources. When a query concerns a business, Bing may show hours and location, with listings that owners can claim through Bing Places for Business in limited markets. The product page adds image search, maps, shopping, news, travel, Image Creator, SafeSearch and a Bing application, and it warns that feature availability and functionality may vary by device type, market and browser version. Personalisation is documented as using search history, location, language and device characteristics, with settings exposed in Bing Settings and search history deletable through the account privacy dashboard. SafeSearch and Family Safety are presented as the controls for what kind of content is returned.
content.installation_and_distribution: Nothing is installed to use Bing on the web. The packaged form is the Bing application, distributed through the App Store under identifier 345323231 and through Google Play under the application identifier com.microsoft.bing; the application page advertises text, voice and image search, daily wallpapers, Image Creator and Microsoft Rewards points earned per search, and states that data syncs across devices. Distribution of the default search position is a separate matter: Microsoft markets its own browser as the best browser for Bing, which is a promotional placement rather than a technical requirement, and the pages consulted do not describe the commercial arrangements that set Bing as the default engine in third-party software. Site owners participate through Bing Webmaster Tools, sitemaps and IndexNow. The retirement of the public search APIs on 2025-08-11 means that developers can no longer obtain Bing results through that programmatic channel.
content.platforms_and_hardware_architectures: The platforms established by the consulted pages are the web, Android and iOS. Desktop and mobile browsers reach the results page; the Bing application is offered for iPhone and Android; and the documentation distinguishes desktop, tablet and mobile contexts when it describes how personal data such as device type is used for relevance. No hardware architecture is meaningful for a remote service and none is documented. Two asymmetries are stated by Microsoft itself and belong here. Feature availability and functionality may vary by device type, market and browser version, so a capability described on the product page may not be present everywhere. And the search engine is embedded in several Microsoft surfaces - the operating system, the Edge browser, the Copilot assistant - whose behaviour is documented in their own terms rather than in the Bing documentation consulted here, so a user's experience of "Bing" may be an integration rather than the web page.
content.extensions_and_add_on_store: Bing has no extension system of its own; it is a service consumed by browsers and applications. The closest analogue on the publisher side is a set of declared protocols and markup directives: XML sitemaps, the IndexNow notification protocol, robots.txt and meta directives, and structured data, all documented as ways to influence discoverability rather than as plugins. IndexNow is the most unusual of these because it is a shared protocol rather than a Bing-only feature: its own site describes it as a way for site owners to notify search engines of added, updated or deleted URLs, states that it is offered under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence, and lists support from Microsoft Bing, Naver, Seznam.cz, Yandex and Yep. The guidelines also state a redirect policy in concrete terms, recommending permanent 301 redirects for permanent moves and reserving 302 redirects for changes expected to last less than 2 days. They add directives that are specific to Microsoft's ecosystem, including notes that NOARCHIVE prevents content from being used in Copilot responses and that NOCACHE limits citations to URL, title and snippet when content is used for grounding.
content.privacy_and_security_model: Privacy for Bing is governed by the Microsoft Privacy Statement, last updated in September 2026, which states that Microsoft complies with the EU-U.S., the UK extension to the EU-U.S., and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Frameworks. The statement describes collection of interactions, including searches and commands, together with device and usage data such as IP addresses, device identifiers, browsing history, error reports and product performance, and it notes that cookies are used for preferences, sign-in, personalised ads and analysis. Bing's own explanation adds how that data is used for relevance: search history, location, language and device characteristics, with user control through Bing Settings and deletion through the privacy dashboard. Safety is described in terms of three commitments rather than technical guarantees: protection from harmful content through SafeSearch and Family Safety, narrow and transparent interventions when content is removed or downranked, and regular transparency reports about complaints and actions taken. These are publisher statements; no independent audit of Bing's privacy or safety practices was located in the sources consulted.
content.update_channels_and_release_cadence: Bing is a continuously updated remote service, so there is no version number to track and no release channel to observe. Microsoft documents change through policy and guidance documents with their own dates - 2025-03 for the explanation of how results are delivered, 2026-09 for the privacy statement - and through webmaster guidance that is revised as the product surface changes, as the addition of Copilot and grounding to the guidelines shows. Ranking behaviour is described as monitored and adjusted continuously, with human judges and oversight, but no cadence, changelog or list of algorithm updates is published on the pages consulted. The Bing application is the exception that does have a release lifecycle, since it is distributed through the two mobile stores and updated there, though neither store listing was consulted for a version number. Site owners are given tools to observe change - Webmaster Tools reports, IndexNow notifications and sitemap freshness signals - rather than a schedule of forthcoming updates.
content.licensing_and_governance: Bing is a proprietary service operated by Microsoft, governed by the Microsoft Services Agreement and the Microsoft Privacy Statement rather than by a source licence; no part of the index or the ranking code is published. The one openly licensed element in the documented stack is the IndexNow protocol, offered under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence and shared across several search engines. Governance of visibility is set out in the Webmaster Guidelines, which describe how Bing discovers, crawls, indexes, evaluates and surfaces content across search, Copilot and grounding results, and which state the consequences of non-compliance: reduced visibility, reduced eligibility for grounding, or delisting. Microsoft's explanation of results adds the principles it applies - credible and authoritative results, respect for local law with narrowly tailored interventions, protection from harmful content, and transparency through published principles and regular transparency reports - together with the statement that sites cannot pay to improve organic position and that Microsoft does not prioritise its own products in algorithmic results, while it may show a separate answer box or banner promoting a Microsoft product when relevant.
content.limitations_and_scope: The limits of what can be known are the same shape as for any large proprietary engine, with one difference in Bing's favour and one against. In its favour, Microsoft publishes a named list of ranking parameters - relevance; quality and credibility, broken into reputation, level of discourse, level of distortion and transparency of ownership; user engagement; freshness; location and language; page load time - and states that they are given in general order of importance. Against it, that list is explicitly approximate: relative importance may vary from search to search and evolve, and no weights, thresholds or feature list are published. Other gaps are documented absences rather than omissions of this entry. The public Bing Search APIs were retired on 2025-08-11, so there is no supported way to query the index programmatically through that channel. Feature availability varies by device, market and browser version. The documentation set does not describe index size, crawl scheduling parameters or infrastructure. And every quality, privacy and safety statement reported here comes from Microsoft; no independent audit or regulator finding was consulted.
content.who_is_it_for: It suits users who want a general web engine with strong vertical coverage - images, video, news, shopping, maps and travel - plus an answer layer that sometimes returns a direct result with sources above the classic links. It suits people already inside the Microsoft ecosystem, where the engine is the natural default and where points earned through searches feed a rewards programme. For site owners it is a required target alongside other engines, and its publisher guidance is unusually concrete about the mechanics of discovery, including the shared IndexNow notification protocol. It also suits readers who prefer a documented list of ranking parameters to a purely narrative account, provided they read the caveat that the order is approximate.
content.who_is_it_not_for: It is not for anyone who needs the ranking system as a specification: the parameters are named but not weighted, and the machine-learning layer is described only in general terms. It is not a privacy-first engine in the sense used elsewhere in this library, since its relevance model draws on search history, location and device data tied to a Microsoft account, with controls rather than avoidance as the mechanism. It is not a platform for developers who want a supported search API, because the public Bing Search and Custom Search APIs were retired in August 2025. And it is not self-hostable: there is no index package, no on-premises edition and no source licence, so an organisation that needs to run or rebuild the engine cannot do so from anything Microsoft publishes.
content.verdict: Bing is the most explicitly documented of the three engines in this batch about how it ranks, and the most careful about the limits of that documentation: it names the parameters, orders them, and then says the order is approximate and changes. That is a more honest position than a list of factors presented as fact, and it should be read alongside the parts Microsoft does not publish, namely weights, features and the training regime in detail. The publisher-facing tooling is coherent - sitemaps, IndexNow, Webmaster Tools, meta directives that now also govern Copilot and grounding - and the IndexNow protocol is genuinely shared rather than proprietary. The costs are the usual ones for a large proprietary service: closed index and code, personalisation built on account and device data, feature availability that varies by market, and the loss of the public search APIs in 2025.
